stances.claim: The complementarity principle (Art. 17) is the primary barrier: the ICC will decline jurisdiction unless the Philippines is 'unwilling or unable genuinely' to investigate/prosecute Duterte — and the dismissal of his impeachment complaint is insufficient proof, because impeachment is not a criminal investigation.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-hurdle identification: distinguishing impeachment from criminal prosecution to rebut the unwillingness argument

stances.claim: The only realistically viable ICC prosecutorial pathway is OSP proprio motu initiation — the Philippines will not self-refer, and China will likely veto any UNSC referral — and even that pathway requires Pre-Trial Chamber authorization that has been denied in prior cases.
stances.rhetorical_move: three-option elimination analysis: ruling out two pathways (self-referral, UNSC) to identify the sole viable route and then qualifying its difficulty

stances.claim: Bensouda's public monitoring statement does not constitute a formal preliminary investigation — the Pre-Trial Chamber authorization has not been sought, let alone granted — making any ICC prosecution of Duterte still very far from initiation.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-status update as a reality check on public misperceptions about ICC progress

notable_anecdotes: Dr. Raul Pangalangan — former UP Law dean and former Inquirer publisher — being an ICC member: CJ notes this Philippine connection to the Court as a quiet signal of the country's institutional investment in the ICC, before proceeding to explain why that investment does not make the Duterte case easy.

The China veto observation — 'the Security Council … given that China will probably veto it' — as a geopolitical realism aside that diplomatically but unmistakably identifies China's protective posture toward Duterte as a structural obstacle to UNSC referral.

CJ's rare admission that he 'ran out of space' before covering Art. 25 individual criminal responsibility — a candid acknowledgment of the column's space constraint that also signals the ICC case's complexity exceeds a single column's analytical capacity.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban systematically identifies the multiple legal hurdles to indicting President Duterte in the ICC for alleged crimes against humanity. The primary barrier is the complementarity principle (Art. 17 Rome Statute): the ICC will decline unless the Philippines is 'unwilling or unable genuinely' to investigate or prosecute him, and the mere dismissal of his impeachment complaint is insufficient proof -- impeachment is not a criminal investigation, and the Ombudsman retains authority to investigate motu proprio and sue him after his term. Even if complementarity is overcome, the three prosecutorial initiation pathways each have obstacles: the Philippines will not self-refer; China would likely veto a UNSC referral; and even OSP proprio motu initiation requires Pre-Trial Chamber authorization that has been denied in prior cases. He notes that ICC Chief Prosecutor Bensouda has only said her office will 'closely monitor developments' -- no formal preliminary investigation authorization has been sought or granted. He closes by noting that Art. 25 (individual criminal responsibility) presents additional hurdles he has no space to address, and that anyone seriously pursuing an ICC case must master three key documents: the Rome Statute, the ICC Rules of Procedure, and the Elements of Crimes.
